interviewQuestions.question: What's the practical difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden, and why do people mix them up?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as identity versus permission. 401 means the server doesn't know who's asking — credentials missing or invalid, fix is to authenticate. 403 means the server knows who's asking, but that identity can't do this — re-authenticating won't help.

The confusion happens because both feel like 'access denied' to a user. Concretely: an admin endpoint hit with no login token gets 401; hit while logged in as a regular user gets 403.

**Testing:** whether you can map each code to the right fix — 401 needs new credentials, 403 needs different permissions.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: 401 vs 403

interviewQuestions.question: Why does HTTP/1.1's persistent connection support matter so much for real-world page load performance?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Under HTTP/1.0, every resource on a page — the HTML, then each CSS file, each image — meant a fresh TCP handshake (and TLS, if HTTPS), pure round-trip overhead before a useful byte moves.

HTTP/1.1 defaults to keep-alive: one connection carries many sequential requests. A page with 30 assets pays the handshake cost once instead of 30 times — on a network with 50-100ms round trips, that's a visibly slower page or not.

**Testing:** whether you connect a protocol-level default (keep-alive) to its concrete, measurable performance impact.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why keep-alive matters
